A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AIS and Stratified Subsampling research despite substantial revision and retitling. All 14 pages of v1 and 12 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures and references, support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: Section 6 and Table 1 report original synthetic regression experiments comparing AIS and SS with other estimators under Gaussian and heavy-tailed noise.

after.justification: Section 5, Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–3 report original synthetic, contamination, named-dataset and runtime results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Huber loss and L1 regularization into AIS, adds uniform-mixture stabilization of its sampling weights, and replaces SS's stratum-level median-of-means estimates with Huber-Lasso fits. It also introduces nodewise-Lasso de-biasing for inference. These are procedural changes beyond the retained AIS and SS names.

E1.justification: v1's reported numerical coverage is synthetic sparse linear regression. v2 retains synthetic regression and adds Riboflavin, Communities & Crime, CCLE-proxy and FRED-MD evaluations, extending coverage to substantially different data settings, including extreme dimensionality and time-series observations.

E2.justification: The synthetic Table 1 comparator set changes from OLS, Lasso and Ridge in v1 to Uniform Huber-Lasso, Lasso and a full-data Huber-Lasso oracle in v2. Thus OLS and Ridge disappear from the reported comparison, while robust uniform-sampling and full-data references become explicit comparators.

E3.justification: The reported synthetic setting changes from approximately n=10,000, p=1,000 and s=5 to n=2,000, p=1,000 and s=10, with m=800 removed. Table 1 switches from coefficient MSE to L2 estimation error. Added dataset evaluations use a held-out 20% test split and five-fold cross-validation.

E4.justification: v1 provides varying-subsample-size scores and largely qualitative convergence and robustness discussion. v2 adds a dedicated contamination-fraction sweep at m=200 (Figure 2), fitted log-log convergence slopes across noise and dataset settings (Figures 1 and 3), and runtime comparisons. These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 states that repeated runs were averaged but supplies neither repetition counts nor empirical dispersion. v2 specifies 20 synthetic repetitions and 10 seeds for the added dataset evaluations, and reports mean±standard-deviation entries in Tables 1–2. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting; it does not establish an increased run count for the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: The synthetic result table is replaced under changed methods, settings and metrics, so its scores are not same-setting improvements over v1. New results include contaminated-noise errors at m=400 of 1.78±0.57 for AIS, 0.99±0.17 for SS and 6.34±0.45 for Uniform Huber-Lasso. Dataset results, measured slopes, contamination-sweep outcomes and timings are also added.

T1.justification: v1's general-estimator and covariance-inversion arguments are replaced by Huber-Lasso score and restricted-convexity analysis, bounded-probability assumptions, and explicit AIS/SS linkage propositions. The claimed estimation rate changes from dependence on n to dependence on m. Mixing theory is reformulated around calendar-time blocks, and raw-estimator normality is replaced by de-biased coordinate inference under a new sparse-precision assumption.

C1.justification: v2 narrows the broad non-standard parameter-estimation scope to sparse regression with sub-Gaussian design and finite-variance noise. It retracts the implication that a small subsample attains the full-data error rate, and instead emphasizes an m-dependent minimax rate. New central claims concern closing the theory-algorithm gap, valid de-biased confidence intervals, and specific contamination and Riboflavin advantages.

C2.justification: v2 adds contamination-floor interpretations, termination-only qualifications for AIS theory, SS's small-strata failure on Riboflavin, and AIS's measured runtime disadvantage. It explicitly excludes infinite-variance noise. It also introduces a mechanism inconsistency: the conclusion says AIS favors high-loss observations, whereas its negative-exponential weights and v1's explanation down-weight them.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously absent regularization scaling with C=0.5, AIS temperature options, cross-validation and standardization instructions, and nodewise-Lasso tuning and construction details. It revises AIS complexity from O(Tmp) to O(Tnp+Tmp) and reports wall-clock timings. Reproducibility remains incomplete: numerical T, alpha, K and Huber-threshold settings, hardware and runnable code are not supplied.

R1.justification: v1's sparse theoretical citations are replaced by substantially broader positioning around robust regression, subsampling, median-of-means estimation and de-biased inference. v2 explicitly presents SS as an instance of the Lecué–Lerasle framework and contrasts its design assumptions with RIGHT, changing the account of novelty and dependence on prior research.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Algorithms move before the theoretical analysis, lengthy algorithm explanations are compressed, and the formerly separate theoretical and statistical analyses become a reorganized sequence of assumptions, propositions, lemmas and theorems. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v1's single gridded results table is replaced by two differently structured tables, and v2 adds three figures covering convergence, contamination, dataset performance and runtime. Algorithm boxes, headings and page styling are redesigned. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates or pagination.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects v1's full-sample-rate overclaim and substantially improves empirical coverage, uncertainty reporting and stated limitations. However, central new guarantees contain demonstrable gaps: Proposition 4.1 incorrectly bounds normalized adaptive probabilities by 1/n, and Theorem 4.12's unrestricted block starts do not ensure the claimed temporal separation. These undermine the asserted theory-algorithm connection and dependence guarantees. The reporting gains coexist with central validity problems, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
